Response to Request for Information: Accelerating Speed to Power/Winning the 
Artificial Intelligence Race: Federal Action to Rapidly Expand Grid Capacity and 
Enable Electricity Demand Growth 
 
Submitted by the Software & Information Industry Association to the Grid 
Deployment Office, Department of Energy 
 
November 21, 2025 
 
Introduction 
 
The Software & Information Industry Association (SIIA) appreciates the opportunity to 
respond to the Department of Energy’s (DOE) Request for Information on “Accelerating 
Speed to Power / Winning the Artificial Intelligence Race: Federal Action to Rapidly Expand 
Grid Capacity and Enable Electricity Demand Growth.” 
 
SIIA’s nearly 400 members, including creators of software and platforms used by millions 
worldwide, are at the forefront of artificial intelligence innovation. Our member companies 
range from global leaders in AI models and applications, companies specializing in data 
analytics and information services, academic and scientific publishers, education technology 
companies, and the global financial information and market data community. 
 
Reliable, affordable, and scalable access to electricity is fundamental to the operation and 
expansion of AI and other emerging technologies. Data centers and AI compute clusters 
require consistent, high-quality power to support workloads that are central to U.S. economic 
growth, scientific discovery, and national security. Companies are investing large sums of 
capital in the United States to expand digital infrastructure, but that infrastructure is only 
viable if it can connect to a robust, reliable, and reasonably priced electricity grid. However, 
speed to power remains a key concern. While power lines can often be physically 
constructed in two to three years, the associated studies, permitting, and siting processes 
can extend beyond a decade. Over the past 25 years, the United States has not experienced 
structural electricity demand growth at the scale emerging today, and the systems and 
supply chains needed to support this expansion are being tested. Capturing the AI 
opportunity in the United States will require both significant investment and meaningful 
permitting and planning reforms. 
 
Across the country, we are already experiencing significant and growing power bottlenecks 
that directly affect data center deployment. In grids without sufficient headroom, new large 
loads can trigger cascading upgrades that quickly expand out of control due to the 
interconnected nature of the system. This reality underscores the need for long-term 
regional transmission lines and backbone infrastructure that can be planned and built in 
 
​
​

advance of load, rather than expanding the grid on an ad hoc, project-by-project basis. 
Because transmission exhibits strong economies of scale, larger backbones built once are 
far more cost-effective than incrementally rebuilding the grid for each new load or generator 
that seeks to interconnect. 
 
SIIA appreciates the Trump Administration’s sustained focus on addressing energy 
infrastructure and AI in order to bolster American leadership.1 These initiatives are essential 
steps toward aligning U.S. energy infrastructure with the demands of a rapidly evolving 
digital economy. However, substantial gaps still need to be addressed to support the scale of 
investment required to support the nation’s emerging AI and data infrastructure needs.2 We 
appreciate that DOE is considering actions to strengthen the federal role in accelerating 
critical generation and transmission projects to ensure the electric grid can accommodate 
and enable this growth. The comments below elaborate on the challenges created by 
bottlenecks in interconnection, transmission, and permitting. We offer specific 
recommendations to improve speed to power, support private investment, and strengthen 
U.S. competitiveness in AI. 
 
Section 3: Use of DOE Funding, Financing, and Technical Assistance 
 
a. In what specific ways can DOE support the development and deployment of large-scale 
generation and transmission projects? Please provide concrete examples and suggestions 
in areas such as: i. Financial incentives (e.g., grants, loans, tax credits, etc.) iv. Streamlining 
environmental review and permitting processes 
 
The United States currently lacks a cohesive national framework to ensure sufficient and 
reliable energy supply for data centers and AI compute facilities. Permitting and transmission 
processes are often fragmented across federal, state, and local jurisdictions, resulting in 
significant delays and uncertainty for infrastructure projects critical to AI development. 
State-level policies can further exacerbate these challenges through inconsistent rate 
structures or discriminatory practices targeting high-load users such as data centers. 
Additionally, the absence of forward-looking federal incentives for low-carbon, 
high-reliability energy sources, particularly nuclear, limits the country’s ability to scale AI 
infrastructure sustainably. SIIA member companies rely on large-scale, high-performance 
computing infrastructure to train and deploy AI models, manage data operations, and deliver 
digital services globally. These facilities are energy-intensive, and uncertainty around power 
availability, costs, and permitting timelines directly affects their ability to plan, invest, and 
expand within the United States. Without reliable access to affordable and sustainable 
energy, U.S.-based technology firms face increased costs and risk falling behind international 
2 Bethany Abbate and Paul Lekas, America’s Energy Grid Needs to Be Ready to Power U.S. Innovation 
RealClearEnergy.org (October 30, 2025). 
1 Software & Information Industry Association, SIIA Commends White House on the AI Action Plan 
(July 23, 2025).

counterparts operating in jurisdictions with more favorable infrastructure and regulatory 
environments. 
 
Lengthy or unpredictable permitting timelines also deter private investment, delay 
innovation, and can push critical AI infrastructure projects offshore, undermining U.S. 
economic and national security interests. Furthermore, disparate state policies and uneven 
incentive structures create regional inequities that distort market competition and limit the 
geographic diversity of AI infrastructure development. 
 
Recommendation: Streamline Permitting for AI Infrastructure Projects 
 
SIIA encourages efforts to streamline federal permitting reforms that simplify and accelerate 
approvals for data centers, high-performance compute clusters, and related facilities. Such 
reforms would reduce uncertainty, attract private investment, and help distribute AI 
infrastructure equitably across regions. 
 
Recommendation: Incentivize Domestic Nuclear Energy for AI Infrastructure 
 
To ensure a stable, low-carbon energy supply capable of meeting AI’s increasing power 
needs, the federal government should incentivize the development of domestic nuclear 
energy, including small modular reactors (SMRs). This can be achieved through streamlined 
regulatory pathways, targeted tax incentives, and federal loan guarantees. Investing in 
next-generation nuclear energy would provide a dependable and sustainable source of 
power for data centers while advancing U.S. energy security goals. 
 
g. What additional coordination is needed between DOE and other federal agencies (e.g., 
U.S. Department of Agriculture, Department of Commerce, Department of Interior, 
Environmental Protection Agency, the Department of Defense, Department of the Treasury, 
Department of Transportation, the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission, etc.) to align 
funding, permitting, or policy with emerging electric load challenges? 
 
Recommendation: Strengthen Federal Authority Over Transmission Development 
 
SIIA supports granting greater authority to the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission 
(FERC) to site and permit interstate transmission lines deemed to be in the national interest. 
Enhanced federal coordination would streamline the approval process for energy 
infrastructure, reduce permitting delays, and ensure a reliable national grid capable of 
meeting growing AI energy demands. Where appropriate, the federal government should 
have the ability to utilize eminent domain to advance projects critical to national 
competitiveness and energy security. 
 
Recommendation: Prevent Discriminatory State-Level Practices

The federal government should implement policies or guidance to prevent states from 
enacting discriminatory energy pricing or regulatory barriers that disproportionately burden 
data centers or innovations in AI-related infrastructure. Establishing a national standard for 
data center electricity rates and ensuring equal access to economic incentives across 
jurisdictions would foster a level playing field for AI infrastructure investment. This would 
also help avoid regional concentration of compute resources and promote more balanced 
economic development in communities across the country as America increasingly 
harnesses the benefits of AI. 
 
Section 4: Load Growth Trends 
 
a. What types of new electric load are driving demand increases in your service area or 
region? b. Please provide any available projections or forecasts of the scale, timing, and 
location of this expected growth. 
 
The expansion of AI in the United States has created a real and sustained increase in energy 
demand for digital infrastructure and cloud computing. While numerous large-scale 
projections have been produced to quantify this growth, they must be interpreted with 
extreme caution. The methodologies currently used to forecast AI-related load growth are 
often opaque, inconsistent, and may not yet be fit for purpose in an era of rapid digital 
expansion. 
 
The scale of projected growth is substantial. For example, based on data submitted by 
utilities, PJM is now expecting well over 60,000 MW of new data center demand by 2030. 
However, these projections illustrate both the magnitude of potential load and the 
deficiencies of current forecasting practices. Many forecasts are built on an aggregation of 
speculative interconnection requests rather than firm, commercially committed projects. 
Developer “shopping” exacerbates this problem: prospective developers may submit 
interconnection requests for the same potential load at multiple utilities in order to secure 
the most favorable terms. Since these speculative requests are not rigorously vetted for 
commercial viability, they can appear multiple times in load forecasts, leading to significant 
double-counting and massively inflated demand projections. 
 
Additionally, there is no consistent standard across utilities and regions. Some utilities 
include 100 percent of a project’s nameplate capacity in their forecasts as soon as a study 
agreement is signed. Others apply non-standard ramp rates or utilization factors that are not 
transparent to stakeholders. This “black box” approach creates extreme unreliability. At the 
same time, while aggregate load growth is both substantial and growing, large-load 
interconnection queues generally do not distinguish effectively between firm plans and 
prospective concepts. Each interconnection request can exacerbate capacity shortfalls and 
overwhelm planning and queue processes, turning otherwise routine interconnection 
studies into decade-long exercises. Similar to generation interconnection queues, load 
queues are attempting to model additions in meshed grids with complex interactive effects,

where each project materially influences the impact of others on both the generation and 
load sides, yet these queues have historically been managed in isolation. 
 
DOE’s recent effort to expedite large-load interconnection via processes at FERC is directed 
at the right underlying problem. However, it is important to recognize that interconnection 
study delays are often downstream of a more fundamental constraint: a lack of regional 
transmission headroom. When the grid lacks baseline capacity, system impact studies 
become more complex, triggering cascading upgrades that would be better addressed 
through long-term regional backbone development rather than incremental project-specific 
fixes. 
Recommendation: Base Forecasts on Firm Financial Commitments 
To address these challenges, forecasting processes should be reformed to include new 
large loads only when they are backed by significant up-front investments and firm financial 
commitments. The current black-box forecasting approach is not a trivial issue. Inflated load 
forecasts are a primary input to regional capacity markets and can lead to artificially high 
capacity costs, potentially on the order of tens of billions of dollars per year, that are 
ultimately borne by all consumers. 
This single change would solve two problems: 
1.​ It protects consumers: It would ensure that billions of dollars in grid investments are 
not made to serve "phantom" loads that never materialize. 
2.​ It enables the AI transition: The multi-billion-dollar investments in new generation 
and data center infrastructure required to power the AI revolution depend on stable, 
accurate, and reliable market price signals. By basing forecasts on economic reality, 
we create the market confidence necessary for developers of both generation and 
load to commit capital and build the infrastructure our nation needs. 
The inability to uplift and fast-track high commitment loads, either with financial or 
long-term contractual commitments, is leading to both capacity markets and large load 
queues. Timely development is only possible when the underlying commitments and 
processes are clear and dependable. 
Section 5: Grid Infrastructure Constraints 
 
a. What generation, transmission, or distribution constraints are limiting the ability to serve 
this demand? b. What are the primary challenges and barriers to expanding infrastructure 
and deploying large-scale generation and transmission projects? 
 
SIIA members face a range of generation, transmission, and distribution constraints that limit 
the ability to serve fast-growing AI and data center loads. At the transmission level, 
insufficient use of advanced transmission technologies, such as high-capacity advanced

conductors, constrains the grid’s ability to quickly expand power flow. Advanced conductors 
such as aluminum conductor composite core can substantially increase current-carrying 
capacity, yet many utilities do not allow large-load customers to finance or deploy these 
upgrades due to technical or process concerns. This limits a practical route for large loads to 
invest in rapid capacity increases that could meaningfully improve speed to power. 
 
Capacity delays also arise from long interconnection study times and persistent queue 
backlogs. In many cases, even where storage or co-located generation could be deployed 
quickly to meet peak needs or provide grid support, regulatory rules make it difficult to use 
these resources efficiently. There is substantial interest among data centers and other large 
customers in investing in demand response and hybrid resources such as solar-plus-storage, 
which can offer additive capacity value for peak shaving and resilience. Yet in many states 
and utility regions, it is not legally or practically possible to develop capacity resources that 
directly increase speed to power or to secure appropriate accreditation and compensation 
for such investments. 
 
On the generation side, nuclear investments are slowed by long lead times for core 
equipment, extended site diligence requirements, and mandatory hearings that add to 
timelines even when they are uncontested. More broadly, grid-related lead times are driven 
not only by transmission overloads but also by delays in procuring and installing equipment 
needed to stabilize the grid. Large-scale transformers can have multi-year delays, and 
STATCOMs and other reactive support equipment often face similar or longer timelines. 
Upgrading lines can trigger the need for this additional equipment, further extending project 
schedules and complicating planning. 
 
DOE can help address these constraints by using tools such as the Defense Production Act 
to accelerate American manufacturing of critical grid equipment, including transformers and 
stability devices. There is an opportunity to leverage targeted investments to pull forward 
manufacturing capacity and grid buildout, but such efforts require utilities to actively 
participate and ensure that large-load customers paying a premium for speed are treated 
fairly with respect to both grid access and the equipment they effectively finance. The fact 
that this sort of market-based coordination is not occurring at scale today reflects a 
combination of cultural, supply-chain, and regulatory barriers. 
 
Beyond equipment constraints, broader permitting and siting challenges for energy 
infrastructure can further stall deployment. The potential for long-term litigation, combined 
with the absence of upfront clarity and predictable processes, significantly increases project 
risk. Identifying ways to reduce this risk, whether through new legislation or via expedited 
and harmonized federal permitting processes and unified siting authorities, will be critical to 
unlocking timely development of new generation and transmission with sufficient headroom 
for future growth.

Historically, the United States demonstrated what is possible in the postwar period, when 
nearly 80,000 miles of transmission were planned, sited, and built within two to five years. By 
contrast, in the modern environment, major lines can take a decade or more from initial need 
identification to completion. These kinds of delays will continue to constrain development if 
left unaddressed. Experience in regions such as Texas shows that where unified siting 
authority, clear jurisdictional lines, and proactive planning exist, it is possible to expand 
transmission infrastructure much more rapidly and at lower cost. 
 
Conclusion 
 
The United States stands at a pivotal moment in the global race to develop and deploy 
artificial intelligence. The ability of U.S. firms to lead in AI depends not only on data, talent, 
and capital, but also on a power system that can reliably and affordably support large-scale 
compute. Today’s interconnection bottlenecks, forecasting challenges, equipment shortages, 
and permitting barriers pose risks to that leadership if left unaddressed. 
 
SIIA urges DOE and its federal partners to adopt policies that modernize forecasting 
methodologies, expand transmission and generation capacity through coordinated planning, 
and streamline permitting across jurisdictions. Doing so will protect consumers, create clear 
investment signals, and support the scale of infrastructure necessary to sustain U.S. 
innovation and competitiveness in AI. SIIA and its member companies stand ready to work 
with DOE and other federal stakeholders to help design and implement solutions that ensure 
the United States can meet the energy demands of the AI era. 
 
Requested Respondent Information 
Company / Institution Name: Software & Information Industry Association (SIIA) 
Point of Contact: Bethany Abbate, Director of AI Policy and Paul Lekas, Executive Vice 
President of Global Public Policy and Government Affairs. 
Address: 1620 I Street, Suite 501 
Washington, DC 20006 
Phone Number: 202-789-4451 
Email: babbate@siia.net 
Primary Area of Expertise: Artificial Intelligence Policy
